cases.holding: The Court held Michigan's one-parent doctrine unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment, so a court may not enter dispositional orders infringing a parent's rights until that parent has been individually adjudicated unfit, and overruled In re CR.
cases.quote: due process requires a specific adjudication of a parent's unfitness before the state can infringe the constitutionally protected parent-child relationship

relevance.INP-04: A judicially ordered CPS referral or petition against only one parent cannot by itself authorize orders against the other parent, who is entitled to his or her own adjudication.
relevance.DEC-05: When the agency files a petition it must name and plead against every parent whose rights it intends to restrict, because jurisdiction over the child does not supply authority over an unadjudicated parent.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective or no-contact orders directed at a parent require a prior adjudication of that parent's unfitness, not merely jurisdiction over the child.
relevance.FAIL-02: Dispositional interference with an unadjudicated parent's custody is a due-process violation and is the leading Michigan ground for undoing such an order.
relevance.PMC-06: Sanders is the structural checkpoint any cross-chain audit should test: whether each parent in a Michigan case received an individual adjudication.

cases.holding: The Court reversed a termination where the incarcerated father was excluded from hearings and his rights were ended essentially because he was in prison, without the court evaluating DHS's efforts or his ability to place the children with relatives.
cases.quote: The mere present inability to personally care for one's children as a result of incarceration does not constitute grounds for termination.

relevance.ACT-02: A court-ordered service plan must actually be offered to an incarcerated parent, who must be allowed to participate by telephone under MCL 712A.19a(4).
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement of a child whose parent is incarcerated does not relieve the agency of engaging that parent in the case.
relevance.ACT-04: The court must consider whether the parent can provide proper care by voluntarily placing the child with relatives rather than treating relative placement as the agency's alone.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification planning must account for a parent's projected release and post-release capacity, not just present incapacity.
relevance.OUT-03: A parent's willingness to place children with kin is relevant to permanency and must be weighed before rights are severed.
relevance.FAIL-01: Mason is the leading Michigan reversal for a court that terminated on the fact of incarceration alone and for the agency's failure to include the parent.

cases.holding: In a lead opinion the Court affirmed reversal of a termination because DHS's and the court's repeated failures to notify the father of hearings and to locate, assess and engage him denied him minimal procedural due process.
cases.quote: A parent whose parental rights have not been terminated, including one who is not a named respondent, must be notified of and permitted to participate in each hearing

relevance.INP-12: Once a child is taken into protective custody, both parents acquire notice rights that attach from the preliminary hearing forward.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal starts the clock on notice duties the agency and court owe every parent, including a non-custodial one.
relevance.ACT-02: Reasonable efforts require the agency to adopt a service plan that actually engages the non-participating parent before dispositional orders issue.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement of the child in foster care does not excuse the state from locating and assessing a non-custodial parent as a placement resource.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts may have to shift to the non-custodial parent's home, and the agency must assess that parent to know.
relevance.FAIL-01: Rood is the leading Michigan authority for vacating a termination on notice and engagement failures by the agency and the court.
relevance.PMC-01: Rood documents the concrete notice and engagement metrics that federal CFSR case-review items measure in Michigan cases.

cases.holding: The Court upheld the then-current MCL 712A.19b(5), holding the trial court may find termination clearly not in the child's best interests on the whole record without assigning the parent any burden of producing best-interest evidence, and reviewed both the statutory ground and best interests for clear error.
cases.quote: Subsection 19b(5) allows the court to find that termination is "clearly not in the child's best interests" despite the establishment of one or more grounds for termination.

relevance.OUT-02: Trejo sets Michigan's two-step termination framework and the clear-error standard of review, though the best-interest step was amended in 2008 and now runs through In re Moss.
relevance.OUT-05: It confirms the trial court may decline to terminate and leave the case open on the whole record even after a statutory ground is proved.

cases.holding: The Court reinstated the probate court's termination order, holding that findings in a termination case may be set aside only if clearly erroneous and that MCR 2.613(C) requires deference to the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility.
cases.quote: An appellate court should not reverse the findings of a trial court in such a case unless its findings are clearly erroneous.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the source of Michigan's clear-error review of a clear-and-convincing termination finding and of the deference owed to the trial judge who saw the witnesses.
relevance.OUT-05: The same deference governs review of a decision not to terminate, which is why dismissals and non-terminations are rarely disturbed on appeal.

cases.holding: The Court held the trial court clearly erred in terminating the rights of a mother who had fulfilled every requirement of her parent-agency agreement, because compliance is affirmative evidence of her ability to provide proper care and custody.
cases.quote: the parent's compliance with the parent-agency agreement is evidence of her ability to provide proper care and custody

relevance.INP-05: A parent who seeks help and then does everything the agency asks is entitled to have that compliance weighed in her favor.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary participation in services is not neutral; Michigan law treats completion of the agreed plan as evidence of parental fitness.
relevance.ACT-02: A court-ordered service plan cuts both ways: non-compliance is evidence of unfitness, compliance is evidence of fitness.
relevance.OUT-01: Full compliance with the parent-agency agreement points toward reunification and makes termination vulnerable on appeal.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the parent has satisfied the plan and the alleged condition is resolved, the case should close rather than proceed to termination.
relevance.DEC-06: The decision supports resolving cases through services rather than escalation when the family is actually engaging with the plan.

cases.holding: The Court conditionally reversed for ICWA-notice violations, holding that almost any indicium of tribal membership triggers 25 USC 1912(a) notice, that a parent cannot waive the tribe's independent rights, and that the trial court must maintain a documentary record of notice and proof of service.
cases.quote: we hold that virtually any criteria on which tribal membership might be based suffices to trigger the 25 USC 1912(a) notice requirement

relevance.INP-11: Morris sets Michigan's very low threshold for ICWA notice and makes the trial court responsible for documenting that notice was actually served.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to give and document ICWA notice is a federal-law compliance failure that requires conditional reversal of the Michigan order.
relevance.FAIL-05: The tribe's separate statutory interest cannot be defeated by a parent's waiver, protecting Indian children from placement decisions made without tribal participation.

cases.holding: The Court held that the relative-placement preference in MCL 722.954a does not apply to a post-termination guardianship determination under MCL 712A.19c(2), and that the trial court permissibly compared placement options using Child Custody Act best-interest factors.
cases.quote: we hold that there is no preference for placement with relatives as part of a guardianship determination under MCL 712A.19c(2)

relevance.INP-05: A relative who seeks guardianship after termination has no statutory head start and must prevail on the child's best interests.
relevance.ACT-04: The kinship preference in MCL 722.954a governs placement during the case, not the post-termination guardianship choice.
relevance.OUT-03: COH is the controlling Michigan authority on how a juvenile guardianship is selected once parental rights have been terminated.
relevance.OUT-04: Because guardianship under MCL 712A.19c(2) keeps court oversight in place, COH shapes the permanency option most often used for older youth who will not be adopted.
relevance.ACT-03: It clarifies the relationship between the placement preference that applies while the child is in foster care and the later permanency decision.

cases.holding: The Court held that a parent of an Indian child who executes a consent under MCL 712B.13 of MIFPA may withdraw it any time before a final adoption order, even in a child protective proceeding, although the department may then refile under MCL 712B.15.
cases.quote: He was therefore entitled to withdraw his consent at any time before entry of a final order of adoption.

relevance.INP-11: MIFPA and ICWA apply together in Michigan, and a parent of an Indian child keeps MIFPA's withdrawal right even inside a child protective case.
relevance.OUT-03: A voluntary release by the parent of an Indian child is revocable until adoption is final, which directly affects whether guardianship or adoption can be finalized.

cases.holding: The Court vacated a termination order, holding that the Department's statutory duty to make reasonable efforts at reunification includes reasonably modifying its services to accommodate a parent's known disability under Title II of the ADA.
cases.quote: Absent reasonable modifications to the services or programs offered to a disabled parent, the Department has failed in its duty under the ADA to reasonably accommodate a disability.

relevance.INP-05: A parent with a disability who asks for help is entitled to services designed so that she can actually benefit from them.
relevance.DEC-06: Front-end, non-court services must also be accessible; an inaccessible service plan is not a real alternative to removal.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary services offered to a disabled parent must be modified to be meaningful, or the state has not really offered them.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans must be tailored to a known disability, and a court must analyze whether that was done before terminating.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification cannot be declared impossible where the agency never provided accommodated services.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to accommodate is simultaneously a federal ADA violation and a failure of the Title IV-E reasonable-efforts requirement.
relevance.FAIL-05: This is Michigan's leading authority on disability discrimination in child-welfare service delivery.
relevance.PMC-01: The case shows how a state's reasonable-efforts performance, the metric CFSR reviews, is measured against federal disability law.

cases.holding: The Court overruled In re Hatcher, holding that a child protective proceeding is one continuous action so a parent may attack adjudication errors on appeal from the termination order, and it vacated the adjudication and termination because the plea colloquy omitted the advice MCR 3.971 requires.
cases.quote: We hold that an appeal of an adjudication error in an appeal from an order terminating parental rights is not a collateral attack.

relevance.DEC-05: Because the petition opens a single continuous proceeding, defects at the front end remain reviewable all the way through termination.
relevance.FAIL-01: Ferranti is the Michigan vehicle for reversing a termination on an error that occurred years earlier at adjudication.
relevance.OUT-02: A termination order rests on a valid adjudication; if the plea taking the court's jurisdiction was defective, the termination falls with it.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the Court of Appeals and upheld the probate court's orders, holding that the Sixth Amendment right of confrontation does not apply in a child protective proceeding and that the statutory procedure for receiving a young child's recorded statement satisfied due process.
cases.quote: because the present case is not a criminal case, we conclude that the Sixth Amendment right of confrontation does not apply

relevance.INP-03: A referral generated from a law-enforcement or multidisciplinary forensic interview can be used at adjudication without criminal-trial confrontation rules.
relevance.INP-06: A third-party referent's report and the child's resulting statements can supply the evidentiary basis for jurisdiction under civil, not criminal, procedures.
relevance.INP-10: The evidentiary rules that govern when a screened report becomes a court case are civil, which is why escalation is easier than a criminal charge.
relevance.DEC-02: Brock frames the whole investigation-to-adjudication sequence as civil and protective rather than punitive.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding may be proved at adjudication with a young child's out-of-court statement under the statutory safeguards.

cases.case_name: Federated Publications, Inc v City of Lansing
cases.holding: The Court held that FOIA places the burden on the public body to prove an exemption, that exemptions turning on legal determinations are reviewed de novo while discretionary balancing is reviewed for clear error, and remanded for application of the public-interest balancing test.
cases.quote: we hold that MCL 15.240(4) of the FOIA specifically places the burden of proof on the public body to show that the public record is exempt from disclosure

relevance.INP-09: An oversight body or requester seeking agency records starts from a presumption of disclosure that the agency must overcome.
relevance.FAIL-06: Non-disclosure is a failure the agency must justify record by record; silence or a bare exemption citation does not satisfy MCL 15.240(4).
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and financial records held by a Michigan public body are presumptively disclosable under the same burden allocation.
relevance.PMC-03: Materials generated by state-mandated review bodies are public records unless the agency carries its exemption burden.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality-review materials held by a public body are subject to the same disclosure presumption and agency burden.
relevance.PMC-05: This is Michigan's controlling statement of who bears the burden in a FOIA dispute and how a court reviews the agency's exemption call.
relevance.PMC-06: Any transparency scoring of Michigan child-welfare data should be anchored to the statutory presumption of disclosure this case enforces.

cases.case_name: Michigan Federation of Teachers & School Related Personnel v University of Michigan
cases.holding: The Court held that public employees' home addresses and telephone numbers satisfy both prongs of FOIA's privacy exemption and are exempt from disclosure because releasing them would reveal little or nothing about the conduct of government.
cases.quote: We conclude that employees' home addresses and telephone numbers are information of an embarrassing, intimate, private, or confidential nature.

relevance.INP-09: Oversight requests for agency records will be trimmed where the material identifies private individuals rather than agency conduct.
relevance.FAIL-06: This case marks the legitimate boundary of a transparency claim: withholding personal identifiers is not a disclosure failure.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit-related records can be released in redacted form, with personal identifiers withheld under the privacy exemption.
relevance.PMC-05: The core-purpose test stated here decides how much of a child-welfare data request must be released and how much may be redacted.

cases.holding: The Court held that chapter XIIA gives the probate court broad authority to enter orders affecting adults, including an order requiring a parent to leave the home, where such orders are necessary for the well-being of a child within the court's jurisdiction.
cases.quote: we hold that the Legislature has conferred very broad authority to the probate court

relevance.INP-04: A court that has jurisdiction over a child may direct adults in the household, which is the statutory basis for judicially initiated protective action.
relevance.ACT-05: Macomber is the Michigan authority for a protective order removing the offending adult from the home instead of removing the child.
relevance.OUT-04: Because the court's power over adults is incidental to its jurisdiction over the child, it ends when that jurisdiction over the child ends.
relevance.PMC-03: The Court also cautioned trial courts to be conservative with orders reaching adults, a limit any review panel examining Michigan practice should apply.

cases.holding: The Court held that after a statutory ground is proved by clear and convincing evidence, the best-interest determination under MCL 712A.19b(5) need only be proved by a preponderance of the evidence, and affirmed the termination.
cases.quote: we hold that whether termination of parental rights is in the best interests of the child must be proved by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Moss fixes the two different burdens of proof that control every Michigan termination after the 2008 amendment to MCL 712A.19b(5).
relevance.OUT-03: Because best interests are decided by a preponderance, an alternative permanency plan such as guardianship must be weighed at that lower standard.
relevance.DEC-03: The clear-and-convincing standard attaches only to the statutory ground, which is what a substantiated finding must ultimately support in court.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination as to three children but vacated the best-interest analysis as to twins placed with a relative, holding the trial court must decide best interests for each child individually and must expressly address relative placement.
cases.quote: We hold that the trial court has a duty to decide the best interests of each child individually.

relevance.ACT-03: Placement decisions for a sibling group cannot be made wholesale; each child's circumstances must be addressed.
relevance.ACT-04: A child's placement with relatives weighs against termination and the court must say on the record that it considered it.
relevance.OUT-02: Failure to make child-specific best-interest findings, or to address relative placement, is reversible error in a Michigan termination.
relevance.OUT-03: Where a child is already with kin, the court must explain why guardianship or continued relative care is not preferable to termination.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed a termination at initial disposition, holding that because termination was sought on the original petition the rules of evidence applied and the grounds had to rest on clear and convincing legally admissible evidence, with the improperly admitted hearsay harmless on this record.
cases.quote: clear and convincing, legally admissible evidence was required to establish the grounds for termination

relevance.DEC-03: When the agency's finding is taken straight to court for termination, it must be provable with evidence that satisfies the Michigan Rules of Evidence.
relevance.DEC-05: Choosing to plead termination in the original petition raises the evidentiary bar the agency must meet at the first dispositional hearing.

cases.holding: The Court vacated a trial court order directing DHS to remove a mother's name from the child abuse central registry, holding that MCL 722.627 vests expunction authority exclusively in the department and that the parent must exhaust the administrative process first.
cases.quote: The plain language of the statute grants exclusive jurisdiction to DHS to control expunction from the central registry.

relevance.INP-09: Registry corrections are an administrative, not judicial, oversight function in Michigan, which shapes where a complaint must be filed.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation from screening to a registry listing is governed by the department's own statutory scheme rather than by the trial court.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out or unfounded closure does not go on the registry; the categories and the registry entry are the department's determination.
relevance.DEC-03: Harper is the controlling Michigan authority on how a substantiated finding gets onto, and comes off of, the central registry.
relevance.DEC-06: Whether a case is handled through services or escalated is reflected in the department's category assignment under MCL 722.628d, which the court may not simply override.
relevance.FAIL-01: The decision shows the limit on judicial correction of an agency determination: the court had no jurisdiction until administrative remedies were exhausted.
relevance.FAIL-06: Registry records are controlled by the department's statutory scheme, which governs both listing and disclosure.
relevance.OUT-04: A registry listing follows a person into professional licensing long after the child's case closes, which is why the exhaustion route matters.
relevance.PMC-01: Registry accuracy is a CAPTA-linked recordkeeping obligation, and Harper identifies the Michigan body accountable for it.
relevance.PMC-02: Any audit of Michigan's registry must be directed at the department, which holds exclusive statutory control of the record.
relevance.PMC-03: A review panel examining registry practice is examining a departmental function, not a judicial one.
relevance.PMC-06: Mapping where registry decisions are actually made is a prerequisite to auditing Michigan's substantiation chain.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary disposition for a physician sued for failing to report suspected abuse of another child, holding the Child Protection Law creates a private remedy only for the identified abused child and that no common-law duty ran to a later-injured third party.
cases.quote: Michigan's child abuse reporting statute creates a private right of action only in an identified abused child.

relevance.INP-01: A mandated reporter's failure to report is civilly actionable only by the child identified in the suspected abuse, not by other children later harmed.
relevance.INP-02: The statutory remedy is narrow, so a non-mandated third party's expectation that a report will protect others has no tort backing.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline report that is never made does not create liability to the general public, only to the identified child.
relevance.INP-08: School staff who fail to report face the statute's criminal and civil provisions, but their civil exposure runs only to the identified child.
relevance.DEC-01: Because the private remedy is so narrow, a wrongly screened-out report rarely produces a damages claim for a subsequently injured child.

cases.holding: The Court held MIFPA's special protections applied to the child taken from the mother's care even though she was placed with a relative, and vacated for non-compliance, but held they did not apply to the sibling the mother voluntarily placed with his non-respondent father.
cases.quote: we hold that the special protections set forth in the Michigan Indian Family Preservation Act do apply to AB's removal

relevance.INP-11: Detmer defines what counts as a 'removal' that triggers MIFPA in Michigan, including a removal into relative care.
relevance.ACT-03: An Indian child moved out of the parent's home into any placement triggers MIFPA's emergency and placement protections.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal of an Indian child must satisfy MIFPA even when the child goes to a relative rather than to foster care.
relevance.FAIL-05: Bypassing MIFPA when moving an Indian child is a failure of the statutory protections enacted to prevent discriminatory removal of Native children.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of parental rights to two Indian children because the trial court's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt finding of likely serious harm was not supported by the qualified-expert-witness testimony ICWA and MIFPA require.
cases.quote: in order to terminate parental rights to an Indian child, a trial court's "beyond a reasonable doubt" finding must "contain" or "encompass" testimony of a qualified expert witness

relevance.INP-11: The qualified expert witness is a mandatory component of the evidentiary finding in every Michigan ICWA/MIFPA termination.
relevance.FAIL-03: Proceeding without qualified-expert testimony is a direct failure of the federal ICWA standard that voids the state court's finding.

cases.holding: The Court held that an employer may be vicariously liable for an employee's failure to report under MCL 722.623 and that the Child Protection Law's good-faith immunity in MCL 722.625 does not extend to negligence or medical malpractice; the Supreme Court denied leave.
cases.quote: We conclude that an employer may be held liable for its employee's failure to report under MCL 722.623

relevance.INP-01: Lee is the leading Michigan decision on the civil consequences of a mandated reporter's failure to report and on the limits of reporter immunity.
relevance.INP-06: Good-faith immunity covers making the report; it does not immunize the underlying professional conduct that preceded it.
relevance.INP-07: Hospitals and physicians face vicarious exposure for staff who see indicators of abuse in a clinical encounter and do not report.
relevance.INP-08: The same employer-liability reasoning reaches institutions whose staff are mandated reporters, including schools.

cases.holding: The Court held that MCL 722.634, which provides that a parent legitimately practicing religious beliefs is not for that reason alone a negligent parent, applies in child protective proceedings, and that respondents were entitled to a jury instruction on it at adjudication.
cases.quote: We conclude that the mandate of MCL 722.634 applies in child protection proceedings.

relevance.INP-01: A report of withheld medical care must be assessed against MCL 722.634, which limits when religiously motivated non-treatment counts as neglect.
relevance.INP-07: A medical disclosure of untreated illness does not automatically establish neglect where the parent is legitimately practicing religious beliefs.
relevance.DEC-02: The statutory religious-practice provision constrains how an investigation of medical non-treatment may be framed.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated medical-neglect finding must account for MCL 722.634's limitation, which the statute makes a merits question at adjudication.
relevance.ACT-06: The same statute expressly preserves the court's power to order medical services for the child notwithstanding the parents' beliefs.
relevance.FAIL-05: Piland protects religious practice from being treated as neglect standing alone, a religion-based fairness limit on Michigan CPS.

cases.holding: The Court held the family court's ex parte and referee proceedings authorizing withdrawal of an infant's life support were fatally defective, that inadequate notice to a respondent is a jurisdictional defect, and it set out the notice, evidentiary and decision-maker standards such a case requires.
cases.quote: The absence of this notice to a respondent in a protective proceeding constitutes a jurisdictional defect.

relevance.INP-04: A judicially initiated protective proceeding is void as to a parent who was never properly notified, no matter how urgent the medical situation.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a hospital's referral about a medically fragile newborn and governs how such referrals must be litigated.
relevance.INP-12: Emergency protective custody does not suspend the notice requirements that give the court power over the parent.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal or emergency order entered without notice to the respondent parent is jurisdictionally defective.
relevance.DEC-05: Every petition must be accompanied by statutorily adequate notice; the defect cannot be cured by the urgency of the request.
relevance.ACT-05: Orders restricting a parent's decision-making authority require the same notice and hearing as any other dispositional order.
relevance.ACT-06: AMB is Michigan's leading decision on the court's authority to authorize or withdraw medical treatment for a child in out-of-home care.
relevance.OUT-06: The child died after hospital staff acted on an order that had no legal basis, and the opinion catalogues every systemic failure that produced it.
relevance.FAIL-02: The Court treated the state's action on a defective order as without legal authority, the paradigm of an unlawful state intervention.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the most detailed Michigan judicial account of a child's death occurring under agency and court supervision.
relevance.FAIL-06: The opinion documents how ex parte, unrecorded and undisclosed process concealed the basis for a life-ending decision.
relevance.PMC-04: AMB is the case a fatality-review body would use as the Michigan template for what post-death review should examine.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may terminate parental rights due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, and vacated New York's use of a fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: Santosky is the federal constitutional floor for Michigan's clear-and-convincing standard on the statutory grounds for termination.
relevance.DEC-05: Filing a petition that seeks to sever the parent-child relationship triggers the heightened federal standard of proof and fundamentally fair procedures.
relevance.ACT-03: The Court held the parental liberty interest survives removal and temporary state custody, which is why placement does not lower the state's burden.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Due Process Clause does not require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the decision to the trial court case by case under the Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.DEC-05: Lassiter is the federal baseline for counsel at the opening of a dependency case; Michigan goes further by statute and court rule in guaranteeing appointed counsel.
relevance.FAIL-01: Where a parent proceeded without counsel, Lassiter supplies the federal framework for arguing that the resulting order must be undone.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from violence by a private actor, so caseworkers who knew of the abuse but left the child at home were not liable under § 1983.
cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney is the federal standard governing whether a child's death or serious injury while known to CPS creates constitutional liability.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is why most claims arising from a child harmed under agency supervision fail unless the state created the danger or took the child into custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Because federal damages liability is largely foreclosed, fatality review and legislative oversight are the practical accountability mechanisms.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held there is no social-worker exception to the Fourth Amendment and that a caseworker may not rely on an accompanying officer to excuse a warrantless home entry, but granted qualified immunity because the right was not yet clearly established in the circuit.
cases.quote: We join other circuits in recognizing that Fourth Amendment standards are the same, whether the state actor is a law enforcement officer or a social worker.

relevance.INP-03: A joint CPS and police response does not convert the caseworker's entry into a lawful police entry; each actor needs a warrant, consent or exigency.
relevance.INP-12: Taking protective custody from inside a home requires the same Fourth Amendment justification that would be required of an officer.
relevance.DEC-02: An investigation that requires entry into the family home must satisfy the warrant requirement or a recognized exception.
relevance.DEC-04: Michigan caseworkers making emergency removals are bound by these Fourth Amendment standards as circuit law.
relevance.FAIL-02: Andrews is the Sixth Circuit's controlling statement that a warrantless caseworker entry is unconstitutional absent consent or exigency.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity to Michigan CPS workers, holding no clearly established law governed a removal that began with the father's express consent and was at most impliedly revoked before a court order issued weeks later.
cases.quote: We find that no clearly established law put the state defendants on notice that they were violating the Bambachs' Fourteenth and Fourth Amendment rights.

relevance.INP-03: The opinion maps the circuit's spectrum, from removal with no order, consent or process at one end to fully consented placement at the other.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody that starts as a consented safety arrangement occupies a legal middle ground where liability is presently uncertain.
relevance.DEC-02: A Michigan investigation conducted under an informally consented placement is largely insulated from damages liability today.
relevance.DEC-04: An emergency removal without a court order is unconstitutional absent consent or exigency, but Bambach shows consent can defeat the claim.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the most recent published Sixth Circuit application of the unlawful-removal framework to Michigan CPS workers.

cases.case_name: Brent v Wayne County Department of Human Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held Michigan's Child Protection Law immunity is an immunity from suit that is immediately appealable, granted state defendants absolute immunity for conduct connected to preparing and filing the removal petition, and reversed dismissal of certain § 1983 and gross-negligence claims.
cases.quote: We therefore conclude, like the Court in Forsyth, that the entitlement under Martin "is an immunity from suit rather than a mere defense to liability."

relevance.INP-01: Michigan's Child Protection Law immunity for good-faith reporting and cooperation is a full immunity from suit, not merely a defense at trial.
relevance.INP-02: A voluntary reporter who acts in good faith under the Child Protection Law obtains that same immunity from suit.
relevance.INP-08: Institutional reporters, including school and hospital staff, can invoke the immunity and appeal immediately if it is denied.
relevance.ACT-01: Service providers who cooperate with the department under the Child Protection Law share the statute's protection.
relevance.FAIL-02: Brent is the Michigan-specific Sixth Circuit case sorting which removal-related acts get absolute immunity and which remain actionable.
relevance.FAIL-04: It shows the narrow remaining path for gross-negligence and § 1983 claims against Michigan child-welfare actors after a child is harmed.

cases.holding: The Court held that the private child-placing agency and its social workers were entitled to absolute quasi-judicial immunity for initiating and monitoring court-supervised child placements, so the trial court erred in denying them immunity, and it affirmed the dismissal of the parents' claims on that ground.
cases.quote: Although we have found no Michigan precedent regarding this question, we find convincing the decisions granting absolute immunity to social workers.

relevance.INP-01: Martin is the Michigan source of the immunity that shields the professionals who carry a suspected-abuse report into the probate court, and it is the state-law rule the Sixth Circuit describes in Brent as an immunity from suit.
relevance.INP-02: Because the protection attaches to the child-protection function rather than to the actor's public status, it reaches private agency staff who act on a report as well as public employees.
relevance.ACT-01: Private contract providers who deliver agency-arranged services and recommend placements share the immunity, so a parent's remedy for a bad service plan is the statutory review hearing, not a damages suit.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination, holding that the ADA is not a defense to a termination proceeding but that the agency's reunification services must comply with the ADA, and that a parent who does not raise a failure to accommodate when the service plan is adopted may not raise it at the termination hearing.
cases.quote: The time for asserting the need for accommodation in services is when the court adopts a service plan, not at the time of a dispositional hearing to terminate parental rights.

relevance.INP-05: A parent with a disability who comes to the agency for help must ask for accommodation at the front of the case, because Terry makes the timing of the request decisive.
relevance.ACT-02: Terry supplies the preservation rule for every Michigan ADA challenge to a court-ordered service plan: object when the plan is adopted, not years later.
relevance.OUT-01: Reasonable efforts to reunify are measured against the parent's known limitations, so an unaccommodated plan cannot establish that reunification was genuinely attempted.
relevance.FAIL-05: Terry is the pre-Hicks Michigan framework for disability discrimination in service delivery, and it channels an untimely accommodation claim into a separate ADA action rather than into the termination appeal.

cases.holding: The Court overruled Fritts v Krugh and held that the probate court's subject-matter jurisdiction is established by a non-frivolous petition on which probable cause is found, so a parent could not collaterally attack the earlier adjudication on appeal from the termination order — a holding the Michigan Supreme Court itself overruled in In re Ferranti (2019).
cases.quote: Our ruling today severs a party's ability to challenge a probate court decision years later in a collateral attack where a direct appeal was available.

relevance.DEC-05: OVERRULED BY IN RE FERRANTI (2019): Hatcher is the source of the collateral-bar rule that once barred a Michigan parent from attacking petition and adjudication defects on appeal from termination, and it must be marked as overruled wherever a search surfaces it alongside Ferranti.

cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of an unadjudicated father's parental rights, holding that the court rules do not require the agency to plead and prove an adjudication against every parent before the family court may act in its dispositional capacity — the one-parent doctrine the Michigan Supreme Court held unconstitutional in In re Sanders (2014).
cases.quote: making it possible, under the proper circumstances, to terminate parental rights even of a parent who, for one reason or another, has not participated in the protective proceeding

relevance.INP-04: OVERRULED BY IN RE SANDERS (2014): CR is the origin of Michigan's one-parent doctrine, under which jurisdiction over the child was thought to authorize orders against a parent who had never been adjudicated.
relevance.DEC-03: CR describes the evidentiary asymmetry the doctrine created — legally admissible evidence was required against the unadjudicated parent while all relevant and material evidence could be used against the adjudicated one — but the doctrine itself no longer stands.
relevance.ACT-05: OVERRULED BY SANDERS: CR allowed dispositional orders restricting a parent who was never adjudicated, which is precisely the practice Sanders held violates due process.

cases.holding: The Court held that circuit courts have subject-matter jurisdiction over third-party custody actions under the Child Custody Act but that a third party gains no standing to seek custody merely because the child lives or once lived with him, and that a court exceeds its jurisdiction by transferring custody from a parent where there is no genuine custody dispute.
cases.quote: a third party does not gain standing to petition for custody under the act because a child resides with the third party

relevance.ACT-04: A relative or kin caregiver with whom a child has been placed does not thereby acquire standing to seek custody, so kinship placement alone does not make the caregiver a party who can litigate for the child.
relevance.OUT-03: Bowie is the threshold standing rule a Michigan relative or proposed guardian must satisfy before any court can consider giving them legal custody, and it is cited inside In re Sanders.

cases.case_name: Bradley v Saranac Community Schools Board of Education
cases.holding: The Court held that the personnel records of public school teachers and administrators must be disclosed under FOIA because information is of a personal nature only if it reveals intimate or embarrassing details of an individual's private life, and performance appraisals, discipline and complaints about public employment are not.
cases.quote: we conclude that information is of a personal nature if it reveals intimate or embarrassing details of an individual's private life

relevance.INP-09: An oversight request for records showing how public employees performed their public duties is not defeated by the FOIA privacy exemption.
relevance.FAIL-06: Withholding records of official performance is itself a disclosure failure, because the privacy exemption reaches only intimate or embarrassing details of private life.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and personnel records bearing on how a Michigan public body did its job are disclosable, with redaction rather than withholding as the remedy for genuinely intimate details inside them.
relevance.PMC-05: Bradley states the personal-nature test that Michigan Federation of Teachers expressly revises, and both halves of that pair are needed to brief the FOIA privacy exemption correctly.

cases.case_name: Herald Co v City of Bay City
cases.holding: The Court held Bay City violated FOIA by refusing to disclose records identifying the final candidates for fire chief, because an application for a public job is not information of a personal nature and its disclosure would not be a clearly unwarranted invasion of privacy, while separately holding that a single city manager is not a public body under the Open Meetings Act.
cases.quote: On its express terms, the FOIA is a prodisclosure statute, and the exemptions stated in § 13 are narrowly construed.

relevance.INP-09: Herald states the interpretive default for every Michigan records request an oversight body makes: FOIA is prodisclosure and its exemptions are read narrowly against the agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: An agency that withholds must fit a narrowly construed exemption and carry the burden of proving it, so a broad or generic privacy claim is itself the transparency failure.
relevance.PMC-05: With Federated Publications on burden and Michigan Federation of Teachers on the privacy exemption, Herald completes the Michigan Supreme Court's FOIA framework of presumption, burden and narrow construction.
relevance.PMC-06: Any transparency scoring of a Michigan child-welfare body should apply Herald's narrow-construction rule when judging whether a claimed exemption was legitimate.

cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and held that MCL 712A.19b(3)(l), which permits termination on the bare fact of a prior involuntary termination, creates an irrebuttable presumption of parental unfitness and therefore fails to comport with due process, and it declined to adopt a saving construction.
cases.quote: As written, MCL 712A.19b(3)(l) provides no way to rebut this presumption of unfitness, assuming the fact of the prior involuntary termination.

relevance.DEC-05: A petition that pleads the prior-termination ground under MCL 712A.19b(3)(l) rests on a statutory basis the Michigan Court of Appeals has held unconstitutional, which is a live defense from the pleading stage forward.
relevance.FAIL-01: Gach is the Michigan decision reversing a termination because the statutory ground the agency relied on could not constitutionally support it.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the only ground pleaded is the earlier termination and the agency cannot prove unremedied abuse or neglect under subsection (3)(i), the petition cannot support termination and the case must return to the trial court.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that parents who voluntarily consent to a safety plan removing their children from the home are not entitled to a pre-deprivation hearing where they never used the plan's stated mechanism to withdraw that consent.
cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them

relevance.INP-12: A child moved out of the home under a signed safety plan is not taken into protective custody for due-process purposes so long as the parents' consent continues, which is the legal middle ground between voluntary placement and formal removal.
relevance.DEC-02: An investigation conducted around a consented safety plan does not trigger the hearing a contested removal would require.
relevance.DEC-06: The safety plan is the practical alternative-response device in this circuit, and Smith fixes the terms on which it is lawful: genuine, continuing, revocable consent.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary services and placements keep their voluntary character only while consent lasts, and Smith places on the parent the burden of using the plan's revocation mechanism to end them.

cases.case_name: Kovacic v Cuyahoga County Department of Children & Family Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of absolute and qualified immunity to social workers who removed children without a warrant, holding that reliance on weeks-old incidents and the mother's missed meeting did not constitute exigent circumstances as a matter of law and that the warrant requirement for seizing children from a home was clearly established in 2002.
cases.quote: The relevant question is whether there was exigency, not probable cause: in the absence of exigency, a warrant is required, even "when probable cause is clearly present."

relevance.DEC-04: Kovacic is the circuit's leading treatment of the emergency-removal decision itself, and it holds that stale information and a parent's non-cooperation are not exigency.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies what Andrews (entry), Bambach (consent) and Brent (immunity) do not: the rule that seizing the children themselves without a warrant or exigency is the constitutional violation, and that a later probable-cause finding does not cure it.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the Fourteenth Amendment claims, holding that a safety plan excuses the state from affording a parent process only where the parent's consent is voluntary and free of duress, and it reversed on the Fourth Amendment claims while holding prospectively that a social worker needs at least reasonable suspicion of abuse to conduct an in-school interview without a warrant or consent.
cases.quote: The only exception to this rule is when a parent voluntarily consents to the terms of a safety plan without duress.

relevance.INP-12: Schulkers materially qualifies Smith v Williams-Ash: a plan the parent signs under threat, or repeatedly asks to have lifted, is not the consent that excuses a hearing before the state separates a family.
relevance.DEC-02: An investigation that imposes conditions on a parent through a prevention or safety plan must still satisfy due process unless consent to that plan was and remained genuinely voluntary.
relevance.ACT-01: Services and restrictions labeled voluntary lose that character when the agency obtains them by duress or refuses to lift them on request.
relevance.INP-08: The Court held the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child in an abuse investigation, requiring at least reasonable suspicion absent a warrant or consent, which directly constrains how a school-based disclosure may be followed up.

notes: Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace, curly quotes and apostrophes normalized) and confirmed to fall inside the majority/lead opinion rather than a syllabus, concurrence or dissent. For Michigan Supreme Court PDFs the Reporter of Decisions syllabus was explicitly excluded by character offset (this mattered for In re Hicks/Brown and In re Ferranti, where the same sentences appear in both the syllabus and the opinion body; the body occurrence was used).

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in every MI_*.json file are keyword-matched noise. All 42 files carry the identical nine titles (In re Barber/Espinoza Minors, In re Contempt of Kathy H Murphy, In re Lange, In re Guardianship of Mary Ann Malloy, In re Guardianship of Dana Jenkins, In re Tracy E. Green Judge, In re Parole of Richard Allen McBrayer, In re Von Greiff Estate, In re Morrow) with synthetic citations. None survived retrieval and review; none is retained here. They should be replaced wholesale.

In re Rood is a LEAD (plurality) opinion: Corrigan, J., joined by Kelly and Markman, JJ., with separate part-concurrences by Cavanagh, Weaver and Young, JJ., and Hathaway, J., not participating. The judgment (affirmance and remand) commands a majority, but counsel should cite the quoted notice rule as '(opinion by CORRIGAN, J.)', which is how In re Sanders itself cites it.

In re Trejo construes the PRE-2008 version of MCL 712A.19b(5) ('clearly not in the child's best interests'). 2008 PA 199 changed the provision to require an affirmative finding that termination IS in the child's best interests, and In re Moss, 301 Mich App 76 (2013), supplies the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard for that finding. Cite Trejo for the two-step structure and the clear-error standard of review; cite Moss for the current burden. Do not cite Trejo's best-interest language as current law.

In re Hicks/Brown (cluster 4389733) and In re Ferranti (cluster 4628995) have NO reporter citation recorded in their CourtListener clusters, so slip form is used per the citation rule (docket numbers 153786 and 157907 were read from the opinion text). Both are published Michigan Supreme Court opinions and both do have official Michigan Reports citations in print; those were not verifiable from CourtListener in this session and so are deliberately omitted rather than supplied from memory.

In re Miller appears in two CourtListener clusters for the same 1989 decision: 1892450 (cites 433 Mich. 331 and 445 N.W.2d 161) and 8000336 (cites 433 Mich. 331 only). The opinion text actually read was opinion 7954381 in cluster 8000336, so that cluster is reported. The parallel N.W.2d cite is 445 N.W.2d 161. CourtListener styles the cluster 'Department of Social Services v. Miller'; the court styles the case 'In re Miller'.

CourtListener's date_filed values for two U.S. Supreme Court clusters disagree with the decision dates printed in the opinions: Santosky (CL: 1982-02-22; opinion: 'Decided March 24, 1982') and Lassiter (CL: 1981-08-28; opinion: 'Decided June 1, 1981'). The dates in this brief are taken from the opinions themselves. DeShaney's CL date and opinion date agree.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used anywhere in this brief. Every state entry is a published Michigan Supreme Court or published Michigan Court of Appeals opinion; every federal entry is a published U.S. Supreme Court or published Sixth Circuit opinion.

Section 1983 / removal: Michigan sits in the Sixth Circuit. Andrews v Hickman County (a Tennessee case) supplies the governing circuit rule that there is no social-worker exception to the Fourth Amendment; Bambach v Moegle and Brent v Wayne County DHS are Michigan CPS cases applying it. Kovacic v Cuyahoga County, 724 F.3d 687 (6th Cir. 2013), and Smith v Williams-Ash, 520 F.3d 596 (6th Cir. 2008) (voluntary safety plans), were retrieved and read but are not included because neither contains a rule statement in the majority that could be quoted within the 30-word limit without dropping a qualifier; practitioners should still read both, Kovacic for warrantless seizure of children and Smith for when a signed safety plan defeats a hearing claim. [SUPERSEDED BY THIS PASS: both cases have now been re-retrieved, re-read, and added with verified majority quotes under 30 words. Schulkers v Kammer has been added alongside them. The earlier exclusion was a formatting artifact and should be disregarded.]

Genuinely thin nodes, where Michigan has no on-point published authority and the entries are the nearest structural or federal authority rather than cases about the node's subject: OUT-04 (extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 - repeated searches of mich and michctapp for young-adult voluntary foster care, MCL 400.641 et seq. and jurisdiction past 18 returned nothing on point; In re COH and In re Macomber are offered for the adjacent guardianship and jurisdictional-limit points, and In re Harper for the post-case registry consequence); FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure - no Michigan decision adjudicates CFSR or Single Audit Act performance, so the ICWA and ADA compliance cases stand in); PMC-01 through PMC-04 and PMC-06 (CFSR monitoring, OIG/Single Audit, Citizen Review Panels under CAPTA 42 USC 5106a(c), the Protect Our Kids Act commission, and cross-chain AI analysis - no Michigan case law exists on any of these oversight mechanisms; the FOIA cases, In re Harper on administrative exclusivity, and In re AMB on fatality review are the closest structural authority and should be read as analogical, not as holdings about these programs).

No published Michigan decision was found on children who go missing from foster care, or on differential/alternative response as such. Michigan's front-end sorting runs through the five-category disposition scheme in MCL 722.628d, and In re Harper is the closest published authority on who controls those determinations (the department, not the trial court). A further targeted search of mich and michctapp for MCL 722.628d category-assignment cases in this pass returned nothing. DEC-06 is now additionally supported by Smith v Williams-Ash, which supplies the circuit rule for the consented safety plan that functions as the de facto alternative response, but DEC-06 should still be read as thinly supported in state law.

Michigan central registry due process: In re Harper holds only that the circuit court lacks jurisdiction to order expunction and that the parent must first use the MCL 722.627 administrative process. No published Michigan decision was found squarely deciding whether that administrative hearing satisfies procedural due process for a substantiated Category I or II listing. That is a real, unresolved gap a lawyer should flag to a client whose name is on the registry.

In re AMB is an unusually long and fact-bound opinion about the withdrawal of an infant's life support. The quoted sentence ('The absence of this notice to a respondent in a protective proceeding constitutes a jurisdictional defect') is a general statement of Michigan law made in the course of holding the family court's proceedings void; the case's specific holdings concern MCL 722.124a(1), referee authority, and the standards for withdrawing life support from a child in out-of-home care. Cite it for the notice rule with that context.

Reporter immunity in Michigan is statutory (MCL 722.625) and narrow: Lee v Detroit Medical Center holds it covers acts done under the Child Protection Law but not negligence or malpractice, and that an employer can be vicariously liable for an employee's failure to report under MCL 722.623. The Michigan Supreme Court denied leave in Lee on March 26, 2010 (SC 139814), so the Court of Appeals decision stands. Marcelletti v Bathani limits the private civil remedy for failure to report to the identified abused child.

Added Martin v Children's Aid Society, 215 Mich App 88; 544 NW2d 651 (1996) (cluster 1991282, opinion 1991282) for INP-01, INP-02 and ACT-01: it is the Michigan decision Brent v Wayne County DHS construes when it says 'the entitlement under Martin is an immunity from suit rather than a mere defense to liability,' so the brief no longer gives the federal gloss without the state source. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to the verifier's description: the Martin MAJORITY (Bandstra, J., with W.P. Cynar, J.) grants ABSOLUTE QUASI-JUDICIAL IMMUNITY to social workers initiating and monitoring court-supervised child placements; it does not construe the Child Protection Law's MCL 722.625 good-faith immunity, which only White, P.J.'s partial dissent discusses. Read Martin for the quasi-judicial immunity rule and Lee v Detroit Medical Center for the separate statutory CPL immunity.

Added In re Terry, 240 Mich App 14; 610 NW2d 563 (2000) (cluster 8005993, opinion 7960556) for INP-05, ACT-02, OUT-01 and FAIL-05: it holds the ADA is not a defense to termination but that reunification services must comply with it, and it supplies the preservation rule — the accommodation claim must be raised when the service plan is adopted — that decides whether a Hicks/Brown argument can be made at all. CourtListener types this single opinion '020lead' with author Cavanagh, P.J.; the cluster (precedential status Published) contains no separate concurrence or dissent, so it is the opinion of the Court.

Added In re Hatcher, 443 Mich 426; 505 NW2d 834 (1993) (cluster 2123972, opinion 2123972) for DEC-05, FLAGGED AS OVERRULED: In re Ferranti (2019) expressly overruled it. Hatcher is included only so that a reader who encounters it in a Westlaw or CourtListener search sees it marked and does not misapply the collateral-bar rule. Do not cite it as current law. Hatcher itself overruled Fritts v Krugh, 354 Mich 97 (1958).

Added In re CR, 250 Mich App 185; 646 NW2d 506 (2002) (cluster 2013344, opinion 2013344) for INP-04, DEC-03 and ACT-05, FLAGGED AS OVERRULED: In re Sanders (2014) expressly overruled it. CR is the source of Michigan's one-parent doctrine and is included only to be marked as dead law alongside Sanders. The opinion is per curiam and unanimous; the quoted clause is from the body of the opinion.

Added Bowie v Arder, 441 Mich 23; 490 NW2d 568 (1992) (cluster 2116959, opinion 2116959) for ACT-04 and OUT-03: it is the foundational Michigan decision on third-party standing to seek custody of a child, cited inside the In re Sanders opinion this brief already quotes, and it is the threshold question for any relative, kin caregiver or proposed guardian entering a Michigan case.

Added Bradley v Saranac Community Schools Board of Education, 455 Mich 285; 565 NW2d 650 (1997) (cluster 1723461, opinion 1723461) for INP-09, FAIL-06, PMC-02 and PMC-05: it supplies the 'intimate or embarrassing details of an individual's private life' definition of 'information of a personal nature' that Michigan Federation of Teachers expressly revises, so the FOIA privacy exemption can now be briefed with both halves of the pair. The quoted sentence is from the majority; Bradley carries a partial dissent that objects to precisely this definition.

Added Herald Co v City of Bay City, 463 Mich 111; 614 NW2d 873 (2000) (cluster 2211455, opinion 2211455) for INP-09, FAIL-06, PMC-05 and PMC-06: it is the third controlling Michigan Supreme Court FOIA decision of the period and states the prodisclosure/narrow-construction default that governs how a claimed exemption is read. Note that its second holding — that a single executive is not a 'public body' — is an Open Meetings Act ruling, not a FOIA ruling, and should not be transplanted into a FOIA argument.

Added In re Gach, 315 Mich App 83; 889 NW2d 707 (2016) (cluster 8007084, opinion 7961848) for DEC-05, FAIL-01 and OUT-05: it holds MCL 712A.19b(3)(l), the prior-termination ground, unconstitutional because it creates an irrebuttable presumption of unfitness, and it is a live defense any Michigan termination brief should carry. CourtListener types Boonstra, P.J.'s opinion '020lead'; Wilder, J., concurred with it (making it the opinion of the Court on the reversal) and Meter, J., filed a separate concurrence whose text CourtListener does not carry. The verifier asked that Gach also be mapped to OUT-02; OUT-02 already holds six cases (the per-node ceiling), so Gach was mapped to DEC-05, FAIL-01 and OUT-05 instead — a reader working the termination-and-adoption node should still read Gach through the DEC-05 entry.

Added Smith v Williams-Ash, 520 F.3d 596 (6th Cir. 2008) (cluster 1201271, opinion 1201271) for INP-12, DEC-02, DEC-06 and ACT-01: it is the controlling circuit authority on when a signed voluntary safety plan defeats a procedural due process claim about the absence of a hearing, and it is the single case most likely to decide a real Michigan safety-plan dispute. The quoted sentence is from the majority; Judge Clay dissented on the ground that voluntariness was a jury question, and Schulkers v Kammer later vindicated much of that concern.

Added Kovacic v Cuyahoga County Department of Children & Family Services, 724 F.3d 687 (6th Cir. 2013) (cluster 1035935, opinion 1035935) for DEC-04 and FAIL-02: it is the circuit's leading treatment of the warrantless seizure of children from the home, which Andrews (entry), Bambach (consent) and Brent (immunity) do not cover. Note this is the 2013 immunity appeal, not the earlier 2010 decision at 606 F.3d 301 (cluster 147186). The quote is from the majority; Judge Sutton dissented.

Added Schulkers v Kammer, 955 F.3d 520 (6th Cir. 2020) (cluster 4740438, opinion 4520785) for INP-12, DEC-02, ACT-01 and INP-08: it materially qualifies Smith v Williams-Ash by holding that a safety plan excuses process only where consent is voluntary and free of duress, and it separately holds that the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child. Read together, Smith, Schulkers and Bambach show that the consent question is far more contested than Bambach alone suggests; the brief's earlier characterization of Bambach as 'the most recent published Sixth Circuit application' of the removal framework should be read with Schulkers in view.

COULD NOT VERIFY (no such authority appears to exist): a Michigan decision squarely deciding whether the MCL 722.627 administrative hearing satisfies procedural due process for a Category I or II central-registry listing. Three separate CourtListener searches of mich and michctapp in this pass ('central registry due process expunction MCL 722.627 child abuse'; 'child abuse central registry Category II procedural due process administrative hearing'; '"central registry" "due process" child protection law expunge') returned no on-point published decision — the only responsive hit was In re Harper itself. This should be stated in the client-facing text, not buried: Harper tells a parent where to go, but no Michigan court has held that the place it sends them is constitutionally adequate.
